content: When evaluating data for risk assessment, preference should be given to international assessments, followed by peer-reviewed regional or national assessments. Evaluations published in reputable, peer-reviewed journals are also acceptable sources. If existing evaluations are used as a starting point, the original study reports should be consulted, especially if they are critical to the risk assessment. Literature searches should be conducted to identify any newly published data, and relevant unpublished studies should also be evaluated and considered. For insecticides that have been in use for many years, human data on their hazardous properties may be available. These data include case reports of accidental or deliberate exposures and poisonings, epidemiological studies (including occupational studies on individuals manufacturing or using the insecticide formulations in question, or general population studies), and ethically approved volunteer studies examining mild, temporary effects of acute exposure or toxicokinetics of the substance in a limited number of subjects. In general, reliable human data on specific aspects of toxicity should take precedence over animal data in risk assessment. Non-active ingredients present in insecticide formulations should also be recognized and accounted for whenever possible. Exposure assessments, however, always consider the formulations. For many pesticides, the human database is often limited. In such cases, hazard assessment relies on information from experimental animal studies and in-vitro studies. For insecticides recently registered or re-registered by regulatory authorities, comprehensive toxicology studies are expected to have been conducted according to modern standards and good laboratory practice (GLP), using internationally accepted protocols for toxicological testing, such as those published by the OECD or USEPA. For older insecticides, animal toxicity data may be limited and may not meet modern requirements unless they have been recently evaluated in regulatory programs designed to review older insecticides. Public health insecticides used in long-lasting insecticidal nets (LNs) have the potential to cause a wide range of toxic effects. To identify the critical effects of the insecticide in question, a range of toxicity studies is usually required. Although test requirements may vary by country, region, or the specific use of the insecticide, the range of tests typically required for health risk assessment (e.g., in regulatory approvals of pesticides and biocides in OECD countries) is generally similar. Toxicity test data are usually available only for the technical materials of the active ingredients or solvents used in insecticide formulations, rather than for the formulations themselves. However, some acute toxicity tests may also be performed with an insecticide formulation. Information on dermal absorption is valuable in assessing the health risks of insecticides used in insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) due to the potential for repeated dermal exposure of users. Inhalation toxicity studies may also be valuable in assessing risks to operators exposed to acute and repeated inhalation exposure. Absorption of the insecticide via inhalation, ingestion, and through the skin should be estimated in the hazard assessment. If no chemical-specific data exist, default values of 100% for inhalation and ingestion are used. For dermal absorption of insecticides with molecular mass >500 and octanol/water partition coefficient (log P OW) <–1 or >4, a default value of 10% is used. Since dermal absorption of several pyrethrins and pyrethroids has been shown to be approximately 1%, it is reasonable to apply a default dermal absorption value of 10% rather than 100% for pyrethrins and pyrethroids when chemical-specific data are unavailable. However, if specific data exist for a pyrethroid, those data should be used instead of the default value. A similar bridging approach could also be developed for other chemical groups of pesticides. If two or more insecticides are used concurrently, possible interactions between those insecticides should be considered. Insecticides with similar actions may produce additive toxic effects (dose/concentration addition); for example, organophosphates reduce acetylcholinesterase activity. For toxicants with dissimilar (independent) actions, the combined effect can be estimated directly from the probability of responses to the individual components (response addition) or the sum of biological effects (effects addition). Other forms of interaction include synergistic (supra-additive) or antagonistic effects, which may be caused by different classes of insecticides, for example, due to metabolic interactions. Synergism is usually only noted at high exposure levels and may be considered unlikely at levels acceptable for the individual components. Dose-response assessment is a critical component of hazard assessment for deriving health-based guidance values and assessing risks. The standard NOAEL (No-Observed-Adverse-Effect Level) approach identifies a single dose assumed to be without appreciable adverse effects. An alternative approach is the benchmark dose method, which calculates the dose at which a particular level of response would occur. These approaches require knowledge of the assumed shape of the dose-response curve. For endocrine-mediated toxicity, the shape of the dose-response curve may not be well-defined, posing challenges for risk assessment. For most endpoints, it is generally recognized that there is a dose or concentration below which adverse effects do not occur. For these, a NOAEL and/or LOAEL (Lowest-Observed-Adverse-Effect Level) can be identified. For genotoxicity and carcinogenicity mediated by genotoxic mechanisms, dose-response is considered linear, meaning that risk cannot be excluded at any exposure level. For non-genotoxic carcinogenicity mechanisms, the critical cancer events may be threshold phenomena. NOAEL and LOAEL values are study-specific dose levels at which no adverse effects or minimal adverse effects, respectively, have been observed in toxicity studies. These values are influenced by study design and the sensitivity of the test system, representing only surrogates for the real no-effect and lowest-effect levels. Different NOAELs/LOAELs are usually identified for different toxicities/endpoints. These can be tabulated for each type of toxicity to help identify the critical endpoint and the critical study. The lowest relevant NOAEL/LOAEL value should normally be used for risk characterization and setting acceptable exposure levels. However, critical effects may not always be the same for each exposure scenario. For example, in scenarios involving high-level acute exposure to an acutely toxic insecticide, acute effects and irritation may be identified as critical effects, whereas effects from long-term/chronic studies should be considered in setting reference values for long-term low-level residual exposure of ITN users via skin and hand-mouth contact. Compounds meeting the criteria for carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, or reproductive toxicity categories 1A and 1B of the Globally Harmonized System on Classification and Labeling of Chemicals are regarded as highly hazardous pesticides. The Joint Meeting on Pesticide Management has recommended that such pesticides should not be registered for use unless a clear need is demonstrated, no relevant alternatives exist, and control measures and good marketing practices are sufficient to ensure acceptable risk to human health and the environment.
